text: Sometimes, partly. If scientists have frozen cells from a recently [[extinct|extinct]] animal, they can try cloning it, putting the cell's DNA into an egg of a close relative. If the animal died out long ago, they can read its ancient [[@dna|DNA]] from bones or frozen remains. Then they edit a living relative's [[gene|genes]] to make it look and act more like the lost animal.

But no one has yet brought back a lost [[species|species]] in a way that every scientist accepts. Clones can be unhealthy. Edited animals are new creatures, not exact copies. And for animals like dinosaurs, there is no DNA left to work with at all.

sec.h: The goat that lived ten minutes
sec.t:
The bucardo was a wild goat of the Pyrenees mountains between Spain and France. The last one, a female named Celia, died in 2000. Before she died, scientists took and froze some of her skin cells.

In 2003, they put her DNA into goat eggs and carried the embryos in other goats. One kid was born alive, the first extinct animal ever brought back. It died about ten minutes later because its lungs had not formed properly. The bucardo became the first animal to go extinct twice.

[[dna|DNA]] starts to break apart soon after an animal dies. Heat and water speed this up, and cold slows it down. The oldest DNA ever read came from soil in northern Greenland and is about 2 million years old. [[mammoth|Mammoth]] DNA has been read from teeth more than a million years old, preserved in Siberian permafrost.

Dinosaurs died out 66 million years ago, more than 30 times longer ago than that. Their bones have turned to stone. Any DNA has long since fallen apart.

The same tools can help animals that are still alive. In 2020, a black-footed ferret named Elizabeth Ann was born in the USA, cloned from cells frozen in 1988. She brought back genes that had been lost from the small surviving population. In 2024, another cloned ferret gave birth to healthy babies.

Only two northern white rhinos are left in the world, both females living in Kenya. Scientists have made embryos in the lab from stored eggs and frozen sperm and hope to carry them in southern white rhino mothers.

Supporters say de-extinction could restore lost [[habitat|habitats]], give us new science and inspire people to care about nature. Critics say it costs a lot of money that could protect living animals, that revived animals might suffer, and that a lab-made mammoth would have no herd to learn from.

Most scientists agree on one thing. It is far easier to keep a species alive than to bring it back. Thousands of kinds of [[@extinction-today|animals are at risk today]], and many could still be saved.

text: Wind is air moving from where pressure is high to where it is low. On a world scale, the Sun does the pushing. It heats the [[equator|equator]] far more than the poles. Warm air rises near the equator, flows towards the poles high up, cools, sinks and flows back along the ground.

If Earth stood still, that would make simple north–south winds. But Earth spins once a day, and that turns the air sideways. The result is a set of wind belts that wrap around the planet like stripes on a ball. In each belt, the wind usually blows from the same direction, year after year.
From the equator outwards, the main belts are the trade winds, the westerlies and the polar easterlies.

st.reveal: Near the equator, warm air mostly rises instead of blowing sideways, so the surface winds are light and unreliable. Sailors called this belt the doldrums.

sec.t:
The first big loop starts at the equator. Hot, damp air rises, building tall rain clouds, and spreads out high in the sky. At around 30° north and south it sinks again. This loop is called a Hadley cell, after the English lawyer George Hadley, who described it in 1735.

The sinking air is dry, which is one reason so many deserts, from the Sahara to the [[@thar-formed|Thar]], lie near 30° north. Some of it flows back towards the equator along the ground. Those are the trade winds.

Two more loops sit further out, between about 30° and 60°, and between 60° and the poles. Each makes its own surface wind belt.

Stand on the equator and you are whizzing east at about 1,670 km an hour as Earth turns. Stand near the North Pole and you are hardly moving. Air flowing across those different speeds gets bent off course.

In the northern half of the world it swings to the right, and in the southern half to the left. This is the Coriolis effect, named after the French scientist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who worked out the maths in 1835.

So the trade winds don't blow straight towards the equator. North of it, they come from the north-east. South of it, from the south-east. And the westerlies, as the name says, blow from the west.

sec.h: Roads in the sky for sailors
sec.t:
Before engines, these winds decided where ships went. In 1492, [[@columbus|Columbus]] sailed south from Spain to the Canary Islands, picked up the north-east trades and rode them across the Atlantic. To get home, he sailed north into the westerlies. Spanish and Portuguese ships used the same route for centuries.

Near the equator lies a belt of light winds called the doldrums, where sailing ships could drift for days. Around 30° there's another calm patch, known in English as the horse [[latitude|latitudes]].

India adds a twist. The [[@monsoon|monsoon]] is a wind that changes direction with the seasons. In summer, the land heats up faster than the sea, and moist winds blow in from the south-west, bringing rain. In winter the pattern flips and dry winds blow out from the north-east.

Arab and Indian sailors knew this [[rhythm|rhythm]] well. For around 2,000 years, traders timed voyages across the Arabian Sea to the [[monsoon|monsoon]] winds, reaching India in summer and sailing home in winter.

Far above the surface winds, about 10 km up, narrow rivers of air called [[@jet-streams|jet streams]] race from west to east. Pilots use them. A flight from New York to London can be an hour or so faster than the trip back. Down at sea level, those same west winds help push the great [[@ocean-currents|ocean currents]] in slow circles around each ocean.

text: A rocket burns two things together: a fuel and an oxidiser. On Earth, a fire gets its oxygen from the air. In space there is no air, so a rocket has to bring its own oxygen supply along, usually as an icy liquid.

Burning the two makes a huge amount of hot gas, which shoots out of the nozzle at several kilometres per second. That backwards rush pushes the rocket forwards. The force is called [[thrust|thrust]]. Rockets use many different recipes, from rubbery solid fuel to kerosene, liquid hydrogen and methane. Engineers choose them for power, price and how easy they are to store.

sec.h: Solid fuel, like a giant firework
sec.t:
The oldest rockets were solid. Chinese inventors were firing gunpowder rockets by around the 1200s. In the 1700s, the armies of Hyder Ali and [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]] in Mysore used rockets with iron casings, which flew much farther than earlier ones. British engineers studied captured ones and built their own.

Modern solid fuel is a thick, rubbery mix of fuel and oxidiser packed into a tube. India's PSLV starts with a big solid stage, and NASA's Space Shuttle used two giant solid boosters. Solid rockets are simple and powerful. Once lit, though, they can't be switched off, a bit like a lit cracker.

Liquid rockets keep fuel and oxidiser in separate tanks and pump them into the engine. They can be throttled up and down, and some can be restarted in space.

Kerosene, a refined cousin of the fuel in old lamps, burned with liquid oxygen in the first stage of the Saturn V that sent astronauts to the Moon. SpaceX's Falcon 9 uses the same pair today.

Liquid hydrogen gives the most push for its weight, but it is fussy. It must be kept at about minus 253 °C and leaks through the tiniest gaps. Fuels this cold are called cryogenic. India's CE-20 cryogenic engine powers the top stage of the LVM3, which carried [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] from [[@launch-sites|Sriharikota]] in 2023.

Methane is the newest favourite. It is easier to store than hydrogen, burns cleaner than kerosene, and might one day be made on Mars. SpaceX's Starship runs on it.

{{story:reusable-rockets}}

Some pairs catch fire the instant they touch, with no spark needed. They are called hypergolic. ISRO's Vikas engine, used on the PSLV's second stage, burns a pair like this. They are very reliable, which matters when an engine must fire after months in space. They are also poisonous, so the ground crew wear protective suits.

A big rocket is mainly a flying fuel tank. Around 85 to 90 per cent of its weight at launch is propellant. The Saturn V weighed about 2,900 tonnes at liftoff, about as much as 500 elephants, and most of that was gone within minutes.

This is why rockets drop empty stages as they climb. Every kilogram of empty tank thrown away means less weight to push. The PSLV, for example, has four stages, and it alternates solid and liquid fuel as it climbs. [[@fire-burns|Burning]] fuel is only half the story. The other half is getting rid of what you no longer need.

In 1920 a newspaper, The New York Times, mocked the American rocket pioneer Robert Goddard. It said a rocket could not work in space because it would have nothing to push against. On 17 July 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon, the paper printed a short correction. It said that a rocket can work in a [[vacuum|vacuum]] as well as in air, and that it regretted the error.

text: Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow along warm coasts, where rivers meet the sea. Twice a day the [[@tides|tide]] rises and floods their roots with salty water, then falls and leaves them in thick mud. For most trees, that much salt would be deadly.

Mangroves have three main tricks. Some block most of the salt at their roots, letting in almost pure water. Some take in salty water and push the extra salt out through [[gland|glands]] on their leaves. Others store salt in old leaves, then drop those leaves. Many mangroves use more than one trick. They also have special roots to cope with mud that has little oxygen. Together, these let them live where no other trees can.

st.reveal: Some mangroves, such as the grey mangrove, take in salty water and push the extra salt out through special glands on their leaves. The water evaporates and leaves salt crystals behind. Rain washes them off.

sec.t:
Mangrove mud is soft, wet and almost airless. Roots need oxygen, so mangroves have found ways to reach the air. Some, like the grey mangrove, send up hundreds of pencil-like roots that poke out of the mud like a bed of nails. These breathing roots are called [[pneumatophore|pneumatophores]]. They have tiny pores that take in air at low tide.

Red mangroves stand on stilts. Arching prop roots grow from the trunk and branches down into the mud, holding the tree steady against waves and currents. In places, the roots form a tangle so thick that even a small boat cannot pass.

sec.h: Babies that start growing on the tree

sec.t:
The largest mangrove forest in the world is the Sundarbans, shared by India and [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]] where [[@rivers-himalaya|the Ganga]], Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers reach the sea. It covers about 10,000 square km, and it is a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]]. Its name is often said to come from the sundari, one of its mangrove trees.

The Sundarbans is home to Bengal tigers that swim between islands and hunt in the mangroves, as you can read in [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans tigers]]. It also has [[@croc-ancient|crocodiles]], river dolphins, mudskippers and [[@crabs|fiddler crabs]]. Millions of people live around it, fishing, collecting [[@honey|honey]] and farming.

India has other mangroves too: Bhitarkanika in Odisha, Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and even the creeks of [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], where mangroves grow beside highways and tall buildings. In the USA, mangroves line much of southern Florida, including the Everglades.

Mangroves protect the coast. Their tangled roots slow down waves and hold mud in place. When a [[cyclone|cyclone]] pushes the sea inland, a wide belt of mangroves can reduce the damage behind it. After a super cyclone hit Odisha in 1999, a study found that villages sheltered by mangroves suffered fewer deaths than villages without them.

Mangroves are nurseries for sea life. Young fish, prawns and crabs hide among the roots before moving out to sea, so mangroves help feed many fishing families. Their mud also stores large amounts of carbon, which helps slow [[@climate-change|climate change]]. Yet many mangroves have been cleared for farms, prawn ponds and buildings. In many places, including India, people now plant and protect them again.

इतना कम ईंधन आता हो, तो स्लॉथ जल्दबाज़ी का ख़र्च नहीं उठा सकता। उसका पूरा शरीर ऊर्जा बचाने के लिए बना है। उसके आकार के ज़्यादातर स्तनधारियों के मुकाबले उसमें लगभग एक-चौथाई कम मांसपेशियाँ होती हैं। उसके शरीर का तापमान मौसम के साथ ऊपर-नीचे होता रहता है, इसलिए गर्म रहने में कम ऊर्जा लगती है। 2016 के एक अध्ययन में तीन उँगली वाले स्लॉथों ने रोज़ किसी भी ऐसे नापे गए स्तनधारी से कम ऊर्जा खर्च की जो [[hibernation|शीतनिद्रा]] में नहीं जाता।
यानी सुस्ती आलस नहीं है। यह सोच-समझकर बनाया गया बजट है। पेड़ पर स्लॉथ की सबसे तेज़ रफ़्तार बस कुछ मीटर प्रति मिनट है, कमरे में घुटनों के बल चलते छोटे बच्चे से भी धीमी।

स्लॉथ के लिए लटके रहने में बहुत कम मेहनत लगती है। उसके लंबे, मुड़े हुए नाखून कपड़े टाँगने वाले हैंगर की तरह टहनियों पर अटक जाते हैं, और इस पकड़ को थामे रखने में लगभग कोई मांसपेशी नहीं लगती। उसके शरीर के अंदर के हिस्से भी इसके हिसाब से ढले हैं। कुछ अंग पसलियों से जुड़े होते हैं, ताकि लटकते समय वे फेफड़ों पर न दबें।

sec.t:
अब सबसे अजीब आदत सुनो। तीन उँगली वाले स्लॉथ लगभग हफ़्ते में एक बार ज़मीन पर उतरते हैं, ताकि अपने पेड़ की जड़ के पास पॉटी कर सकें। यह उनका सबसे ख़तरनाक काम है, क्योंकि ज़मीन पर वे धीरे-धीरे रेंगते हैं और आसानी से पकड़े जा सकते हैं।

वे यह ख़तरा क्यों उठाते हैं, यह किसी को पक्का पता नहीं। एक अनुमान इसे रोओं वाले पतंगों से जोड़ता है। पतंगे स्लॉथ की पॉटी में अंडे देते हैं, और उनके बच्चे बाद में उड़कर स्लॉथ के रोओं में रहने आ जाते हैं। कुछ वैज्ञानिक मानते हैं कि इससे काई को उगने में मदद मिलती है। दूसरे इससे सहमत नहीं हैं, और यह सवाल अब भी खुला है।

स्लॉथ को नदी में डाल दो, तो वह बदल जाता है। वह अपनी लंबी बाँहों से पानी काटता है और ज़मीन पर जितना तेज़ चलता है, उससे कई गुना तेज़ तैरता है। स्लॉथ अपना दिल धीमा करके लंबे समय तक पानी के अंदर भी रह सकता है, कुछ रिपोर्टों के मुताबिक 40 मिनट तक।

हर बरसात में बाढ़ से भर जाने वाले जंगलों में यह बड़े काम आता है। स्लॉथ जितने दिखते हैं, उससे ज़्यादा सख़्तजान भी हैं। वे ऊँचे पेड़ों से गिरकर भी बच जाते हैं, उनके घाव जल्दी भरते हैं, और वे दशकों तक जीते हैं। चिड़ियाघरों में कुछ दो उँगली वाले स्लॉथ 40 साल से भी ज़्यादा जिए हैं।

और सबसे अजीब बात? आज के स्लॉथ छोटे हैं, पर बहुत पहले की बात नहीं, उनके रिश्तेदार हाथियों जितने भारी दानव थे, जो अमेरिकी महाद्वीपों में ज़मीन पर चलते थे। उनकी कहानी [[@giant-sloths|ज़मीन पर चलने वाले विशाल स्लॉथ]] में पढ़ो।

text: The wood frog, a small brown frog from North America, survives winter by freezing almost solid. When the cold arrives, it tucks itself under fallen leaves on the forest floor. Ice begins to form on its skin, and up to about two-thirds of the water in its body turns to ice. Its heart stops. It stops breathing. If you picked one up, it would feel like a frozen pebble.

The trick is sugar. The frog's liver floods its cells with glucose, which works as antifreeze. Ice forms only in the spaces between cells, not inside them. When spring comes, the frog thaws, its heart starts beating again, and it hops off to find a mate.

st.prompt: How does a wood frog stop ice from destroying the inside of its cells?

options.t: It floods its cells with sugar
It swallows warm mud

st.reveal: As ice starts to form on its skin, the frog's liver pours out huge amounts of glucose, a sugar. The sugar packs into cells, so the water inside them doesn't freeze into sharp crystals. Ice forms in the spaces around the cells instead.

sec.t:
Wood frogs live farther north than any other North American frog, all the way into [[@alaska|Alaska]] and beyond the Arctic Circle. They don't burrow deep or hide in ponds like many [[@frogs-world|frogs]]. They spend the winter in shallow leaf litter, where temperatures drop far below freezing.

Once ice touches its skin, the frog reacts within minutes. Its liver turns stored [[starch|starch]] into glucose and pours it into the blood. Sugar levels can rise to many times their normal level, a level that would be dangerous for a person. The sugar soaks into the cells and keeps them from losing too much water or forming ice inside.

sec.h: Why ice inside cells is deadly

sec.t:
For a long time, scientists studied wood frogs in labs, where they survived about −3 to −6 °C. Then researchers in Alaska tracked frogs in their real winter homes. In a study published in 2014, the Alaskan frogs survived about −18 °C, colder than a home freezer.

They also stayed frozen for a very long time. Some frogs spent more than half the year frozen, with short thaws only in spring. During that time, they did not eat, drink, breathe or move.

When the weather warms, the frog thaws. Within hours, its heart starts to flutter. Then it begins breathing, and soon it can move. Within a day or so, it is hopping again.

Wood frogs then rush to ponds of fresh snowmelt to breed. Their call sounds like a quacking duck. The tadpoles have to grow fast, before the shallow ponds dry up in summer. Wood frogs are among the first frogs to call in spring, sometimes while patches of ice still float on the water. Breeding so early gives their tadpoles a head start.

When doctors move a heart or kidney from one person to another in a [[@transplants|transplant]], they have only hours before the organ is damaged. Freezing organs usually destroys them, for the same reason ice destroys cells.

Scientists study the wood frog's sugar trick to learn how organs might one day be stored longer. And the strangest part? Some tiny animals can survive freezing, drying out and even a trip into outer space, as the story of the [[@extreme-toughest-animal|toughest animal]] shows.

text: साड़ी [[loom|करघे]] पर बुनी जाती है, एक ऐसा ढाँचा जो सैकड़ों या हज़ारों धागों को कसकर थामे रहता है। साड़ी की लंबाई में चलने वाले लंबे धागों को ताना कहते हैं। बुनकर उनके आर-पार एक और धागा गुज़ारता है, जिसे बाना कहते हैं, जो कुछ ताने के धागों के ऊपर से और कुछ के नीचे से जाता है। कतार-दर-कतार कपड़ा बढ़ता जाता है।

[[weaving|बुनाई]] में नमूने बनाने के लिए बुनकर हर कतार में ताने के अलग-अलग धागे उठाता है, या कुछ ख़ास जगहों पर रंगीन या सुनहरे धागे जोड़ता है। एक सादी [[@clothes-cotton|सूती साड़ी]] दिन-दो दिन में बुनी जा सकती है। भरपूर नमूनों वाली रेशमी शादी की साड़ी में बुनकरों की एक टोली को हफ़्ते या महीने लग सकते हैं।

sec.t:
बुनाई शुरू होने से पहले ताना तैयार करना पड़ता है। हज़ारों धागे, हर एक शायद 6 से 9 मीटर लंबा, बिल्कुल सही क्रम में ताने जाते हैं और करघे पर लपेटे जाते हैं। सिर्फ़ इसी में कई दिन लग सकते हैं।

[[@knitting-weaving|पारंपरिक गड्ढा करघे]] पर बुनकर एक उथले गड्ढे के किनारे बैठता है, नीचे पैर से दबाने वाली पट्टियाँ होती हैं। एक पट्टी दबाने से ताने के कुछ धागे उठ जाते हैं और बीच में एक जगह बनती है, जिसे शेड कहते हैं। बुनकर बाने का धागा लिए ढरकी उस जगह से फेंकता है, फिर कंघी जैसी हत्थी आगे खींचकर उसे कसकर बिठाता है। फिर अगली पट्टी, अगली फेंक, अगली ठोक, हज़ारों बार।

[[@varanasi|वाराणसी]] में बुनकर [[@art-banarasi|बनारसी साड़ियाँ]] बनाते हैं, जिनमें *[[@art-zardozi|ज़री]]* से फूलों, बेलों और कैरी के नमूने बनते हैं। ज़री पतली धातु लिपटा धागा है, जो सोने या चाँदी जैसा दिखता है। ये डिज़ाइन अतिरिक्त बाने के धागों से बुनकर डाले जाते हैं, इसलिए ये कपड़े का ही हिस्सा होते हैं, ऊपर से काढ़े हुए नहीं।

एक भारी बनारसी ज़री की साड़ी में कुछ हफ़्तों से लेकर कई महीने लग सकते हैं। परिवार डिज़ाइन और हुनर माँ-बाप से बच्चों तक पहुँचाते हैं, और बहुत सी साड़ियाँ [[@weddings-india|शादी]] में दुल्हनों के लिए जाती हैं।

तमिलनाडु के कांचीपुरम में बुनकर मोटी, चमचमाती [[@silk|रेशमी]] साड़ियाँ बनाते हैं, जिनकी चौड़ी किनारी उलटे रंग की होती है। *कोरवई* नाम के तरीके में किनारी और बीच का हिस्सा अलग-अलग बुनकर हाथ से आपस में गूँथे जाते हैं, इसलिए जोड़ बहुत मज़बूत होता है। परंपरा कहती है कि अच्छी कांचीपुरम साड़ी पीढ़ियों तक चलती है।

गुजरात के पाटण में कुछ परिवार [[@art-ikat|दोहरे इकत]] से पटोला साड़ियाँ बुनते हैं। ताने और बाने, दोनों का हर धागा बुनाई से पहले हिस्सों में बाँधकर रंगा जाता है, इसलिए नमूना तभी उभरता है जब धागे आपस में मिलते हैं। रँगाई में ज़रा-सी चूक कपड़े में धुँधले धब्बे की तरह दिखती है।

आज बहुत सी साड़ियाँ, और बाकी [[textile|वस्त्र]] भी, पावरलूम पर बनते हैं, यानी मशीन वाले करघे, जो बहुत तेज़ चलते हैं और सस्ते पड़ते हैं। वे हथकरघे के डिज़ाइनों की बड़ी बारीकी से नकल कर सकते हैं।

हथकरघा बुनकरों के लिए मुक़ाबला करना मुश्किल है, और बुनकर परिवारों के बहुत से नौजवान अब दूसरा काम चुनते हैं। उनका साथ देने के लिए भारत हर 7 अगस्त को राष्ट्रीय हथकरघा दिवस मनाता है। यह तारीख़ 1905 में इसी दिन शुरू हुए स्वदेशी आंदोलन की याद दिलाती है, जब भारतीयों से देश में बना कपड़ा ख़रीदने को कहा गया था। अब कुछ साड़ियों पर हैंडलूम मार्क का लेबल लगता है, ताकि ख़रीदार फ़र्क पहचान सकें।

text: When girls and women reach a certain age, their bodies have a monthly period, a few days of light bleeding that is a normal part of [[@puberty-basics|growing up]]. For that, most people use a sanitary pad. In the 1990s, pads in India were expensive, and many women used old cloth instead, which can cause [[infection|infections]] if it isn't clean.

Arunachalam Muruganantham, a workshop welder from Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu, decided to fix this. After years of failures, he built a simple machine that lets a small group of people make good pads cheaply. He sold his machines mostly to groups of village women, who make and sell the pads themselves.

st.reveal: He mostly sold machines to women's groups. That way the pads are made close to where they're needed, cost less, and the women who make them earn a living.

myth: Periods are something to be ashamed of, so nobody should talk about them.

Periods are a normal, healthy part of growing up for about half of all people. Not talking about them made it harder for girls to get pads, stay in school and stay healthy. Asking a parent, teacher or doctor is always fine.
facts: Women aged 15 to 24 using hygienic methods

sec.t:
Around 1998, Muruganantham saw his wife Shanthi hiding a dirty rag. She told him that if she bought pads, the family couldn't afford milk. He bought a packet to give her and was shocked: a few grams of cotton were being sold at a high price.

He tried making pads from cotton, and they failed. The trouble was that almost no woman would test them or talk about them. So he wore one himself, with a rubber pouch of animal blood under his clothes to see how it worked. People in his village thought he had gone mad. For a while, his wife and mother moved out.

Muruganantham could have sold his design to a large company and become rich. Instead he sold machines mostly to women's self-help groups and charities. Each machine gives work to a handful of women, who buy the materials, make the pads and sell them to neighbours. That is a different way of thinking about [[@startups-entrepreneurs|business]]: the aim is to spread the work, not keep it.

His machines spread across India and to other countries. In 2014 TIME magazine named him one of the 100 most influential people in the world. In 2016 India gave him the Padma Shri.

Part of Muruganantham's work has simply been getting people to talk. For years, many girls in India missed school during their periods, partly because schools lacked clean toilets and pads. Many state governments now hand out free or cheap pads to schoolgirls, and lessons about growing up are part of health education in many schools.

sec.h: From a village to the movies
sec.t:
In 2018 Bollywood released *PadMan*, a film based on his story. The same year, a short documentary called *Period. End of Sentence.* followed women running one of his machines in a village near Hapur in Uttar Pradesh. It won an Oscar in 2019.

Things have changed a lot. India's national health survey found that about 58 percent of women aged 15 to 24 used hygienic methods in 2015–16, rising to about 77 percent in 2019–21. Since 2019, government medicine shops have sold pads for one rupee each. Good [[@public-health|public health]] often looks like this: small, cheap and close to home.

And Muruganantham isn't the only Indian who changed lives with a stubborn idea. A man in Assam once planted a whole forest, tree by tree, on a bare sandbank, and you can meet him in the story of the [[@india-forest-man|forest man]].

text: The USA holds a big national election every two years. Every fourth year, Americans choose a president. In the years in between, halfway through the president's term, they choose members of Congress, the body that makes the country's [[federal|federal]] laws, the ones for the whole nation. These in-between votes are called midterm elections.

The president is not on the ballot. But if voters hand Congress to the other party, the president suddenly needs their votes to pass laws or spend money. That is why midterms are often called a report card on the president.

quiz.prompt: A president wants a new law, but the other party now controls both the House and the Senate. What is most likely to happen?

options.t: The president must bargain with the other party, or the law will not pass
The president can pass the law alone by signing an order
A new presidential election is held straight away

quiz.reveal: In the USA, only Congress can pass laws. A president can sign or veto a bill, but cannot write one into law alone. When the other party controls Congress, the president has to bargain, give something up or wait.

news.h: Americans vote in the 2026 midterm elections for the US Congress
news.t: Americans voted on 3 November 2026, choosing all 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 senators. News reports, including Reuters, said the Democratic Party had won enough seats to lead both the House and the Senate, which President Donald Trump's Republican Party had led before. In a large survey of voters by the AP news agency, about 7 in 10 said Congress was not doing enough to check the president's power. For the next two years, the president will need the other party's votes to pass laws, which could shape US decisions on tariffs and trade, including with India. This entry explains how midterms work and why they matter so much.

d.try: Look at India's next election calendar and find which states vote this year. Then ask an adult whether India has anything like a midterm. Hint, state elections happen at different times, and many people read them as a mood check on the national government.
myth: Midterm elections can remove the president from office.

The president's name is not on the ballot in a midterm. The president stays for the full four-year term. What changes is who controls Congress, which decides how easy or hard the president's job will be.
facts: two years into a president's four-year term, in early November
all 435, because House members serve two-year terms
about one-third of 100, because senators serve six-year terms
many state governors, state lawmakers and local officials
two-thirds of both the House and the Senate

sec.t:
[[@congress-usa|Congress]] has two parts. The House of Representatives has 435 members, and each serves just two years, so every single seat is up for election in a midterm. The Senate has 100 members, two from each state, and each serves six years. Their terms are staggered, so only about one-third face voters at a time.

Think of a school with a head teacher and a student council. The head teacher is chosen for four years. The council is chosen every two years. The head teacher can suggest new rules, but the council must agree before any rule is made.

So a midterm can change everything. If the president's party keeps both chambers, the president can usually pass big plans. If the other party wins one or both, the president must bargain, compromise or give up. Americans call this "divided government".

On the same day, many states also choose governors, state lawmakers, judges and local officials. Some states even ask voters to decide questions directly, a little like a [[referendum|referendum]].

The rules come from the [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]], written in 1787. Its writers wanted the House to stay close to ordinary people, so they gave it short two-year terms. They made the Senate calmer and slower, with six-year terms. The president got four years.

Those three numbers, two, four and six, were never planned to create midterms. They simply did. The first Congress met in 1789, and Americans have voted every two years since, even during the Civil War and both World Wars.

The idea of "checks and balances" sits underneath it all. In a healthy [[democracy|democracy]], no single person or group should hold all the power, so each part of government can slow down the others. The president can [[veto|veto]], or reject, a law. Congress can override that veto, but only with two-thirds of both chambers.

{{story:us-constitution}}

India has no exact midterm, because India runs a [[@parliament-india|parliamentary system]]. Here the Prime Minister comes from whichever party or group controls the Lok Sabha. Lose that majority, and you lose the job. In the USA, the [[@president-pm|president and the lawmakers]] are chosen separately, so a president can stay in office while the other party runs Congress.

The closest thing India has is the steady stream of state elections. Because different states vote in different years, each round is often read as a mood check on the government in Delhi.

US midterms still matter to India. Congress votes on trade rules, defence deals and visa laws, such as the H-1B work visas used by many Indian engineers. It also watches how a president uses [[tariff|tariffs]], the taxes put on goods arriving from abroad. In 2025, US tariffs on many Indian goods went up to 50%, before an early deal in 2026 brought them down to 18%. That is why Indian exporters follow these results closely, because [[@trade-world|trade]] between the two countries is worth billions of dollars.

The first person of Indian birth to sit in Congress was Dalip Singh Saund, a farmer from Punjab, elected in 1956.

- 435 and 35: in 2026, every House seat and 35 of the 100 Senate seats were up for election. That is why one day can flip a whole chamber.
- 2 of about 20: since 1946, the president's party has gained House seats in a midterm only twice, in 1998 and 2002. Losing seats is the normal pattern.
- About half: in 2018, roughly half of eligible Americans voted in the midterm, the highest share in over 100 years. In recent presidential years, about 6 in 10 or more have voted.
- Two-thirds: the share of both chambers needed to override a president's veto. A party with a small majority cannot do it alone.
- 43 days: the longest government shutdown, in 2025. It happened because Congress and the president could not agree on a spending law, so many offices closed and workers went unpaid.

Some Americans like divided government. They say it forces the two parties to talk, stops sudden swings and protects against any one leader growing too powerful. Others say it causes "gridlock", where nothing gets done, budgets are late and important problems are left waiting.

People also argue about how voting districts are drawn. In many states, politicians draw the map of House districts themselves. Critics say some maps are shaped to help one party win more seats than its votes deserve. Supporters of the current system say elected officials are accountable to voters, while courts can step in when maps break the law.

There is debate, too, over what a midterm really means. Some see it as a clear [[verdict|verdict]] on the president. Others say local issues, candidates and turnout matter just as much.

**"The president is chosen in a midterm."** No. The president's name is not on the ballot. The [[@elections-usa|presidential election]] comes two years later.

**"Only the House changes."** The Senate changes too, but more slowly. Only about a third of senators face voters each time, so the Senate is harder to flip.

**"If Congress is against the president, the president is powerless."** Not quite. The president still runs the government, commands the armed forces, leads foreign policy and can veto laws. But passing new laws and setting budgets becomes much harder.

What happens in Washington can reach an Indian family's kitchen table. US decisions on tariffs affect which Indian goods sell well in America, from shrimp and jewellery to medicines and clothes. That touches jobs in places like Tiruppur, Surat and Visakhapatnam.

Visa rules affect Indian students and workers who hope to study or work in the USA. And when the world's biggest [[economy|economy]] changes direction, markets, the rupee and even fuel prices can move.

Next time you hear the word "midterm", remember the school council. The head teacher has not changed, but who must agree to the rules just might have.

text: Propaganda is information spread to push people towards a belief or action, usually for a political cause, often by playing on feelings instead of giving balanced facts. Governments, armies, parties and other groups have all used it.

Unlike honest argument, propaganda doesn't want you to weigh up both sides. It repeats simple slogans, uses powerful images, picks out enemies and makes one choice feel like the only one. It can contain [[@truth-lies|lies]], but often it uses half-truths: real facts, carefully selected. Learning to spot it is a big part of thinking for yourself.

st.prompt: A poster says "Every true patriot supports our plan." Which propaganda trick is it using?

options.t: Linking a plan to a feeling, so disagreeing seems disloyal
Giving detailed facts and figures
Showing both sides of the argument

st.reveal: The poster offers no reasons. It ties the plan to a powerful word, patriot, so anyone who questions it feels like a traitor. Spotting this move is a good first step to thinking for yourself.

sec.t:
In 1622, the Catholic Church in Rome set up an office to spread the faith to new lands. Its Latin name included the word *propaganda*, meaning "to be spread". For centuries the word simply meant spreading a belief.

That changed with the two world wars. Governments realised that [[@journalism|newspapers]], posters, radio and films could move whole nations. Afterwards, people grew suspicious of the way they had been persuaded, and propaganda became a word for manipulation.

In Germany in the 1930s, the Nazi party set up a whole ministry for propaganda. It controlled newspapers, radio and films, burned books it disliked, and spread hatred of Jewish people and other groups. Years of repeated lies helped make terrible crimes, including the [[@holocaust|Holocaust]], seem acceptable to many ordinary people.

During the [[@cold-war|Cold War]], the USA and the Soviet Union each used radio, films and even sports to show their own system as the best. George Orwell's novel *Nineteen Eighty-Four*, published in 1949, imagined a state where the government rewrote history every day. Terms from the book, like "Big Brother", are still used.

In 1937, a group of American teachers and researchers, the Institute for Propaganda Analysis, listed seven common tricks. Among them were name-calling, attaching nasty labels to opponents; glittering generalities, using shiny words like "freedom" without saying what they mean; and the bandwagon, telling you everyone else already agrees.

Many of these tricks also appear in [[@advertising|advertising]]. Today, propaganda spreads on social media, through memes, edited videos and accounts that pretend to be ordinary people. Some uses [[@fake-news|fake news]] or AI-made images.

People often call any message they disagree with propaganda, which can make the word less useful. A better test is to ask some questions. Who made this, and what do they want? Does it give reasons, or only feelings? What might it be leaving out? Does it treat a group of people as less than human?

During India's freedom struggle, both the British government and Indian nationalists used newspapers, songs and pamphlets to win people over. Looking at how each side told the story is a good way to practise.

text: Special effects are tricks that show things on screen that could not really be filmed, or would be too dangerous or costly. There are two main kinds. Practical effects happen in front of the camera: models, make-up, puppets, fake snow and wires that lift actors. Visual effects, or VFX, are added later on a computer.
Most modern films mix both. An actor might stand in front of a green screen holding a real sword, while a computer adds the castle, the dragon and the storm. Done well, you never notice the join.

st.reveal: The computer-made dinosaurs are on screen for only a few minutes in total. Many other dinosaur shots used giant robot puppets called animatronics, built by Stan Winston's workshop, which actors could touch and react to.

Many films still use real models, make-up, puppets, fake rain and controlled explosions, called practical effects. Computers are often used to clean up or add to them, not to replace them.
facts: 1993, only a few minutes of computer dinosaurs

sec.t:
Georges Méliès was a [[@pop-magic-shows|stage magician]] in Paris. According to his own story, his camera jammed one day while filming a street. When it started again, the scene had changed, so on screen a bus seemed to become a hearse. He realised a camera could do [[@magic-tricks|magic tricks]] no stage could.

Méliès used stopping and starting, double exposures (filming twice on the same strip) and painted sets. In *A Trip to the Moon* (1902), a rocket lands in the eye of the Man in the Moon. That image is still one of the best known in film history.

To put actors in a place that does not exist, film crews shoot them in front of a plain screen of one colour, usually bright green or blue. Software then picks out every [[@pixels|pixel]] of that colour and replaces it with another picture. This is called chroma key. TV weather forecasters use the same method to stand in front of moving maps.

Green is popular because it is far from any human skin tone, and digital [[@cameras-how|cameras]] pick up green especially clearly. Blue is used when a character is wearing green. An actor who wears a green shirt by mistake ends up with a hole in their body.

Computer graphics, or CGI, grew in the 1980s and 1990s. In *Jurassic Park* (1993), computer-made dinosaurs looked real enough to stun audiences, though most dinosaur shots used robot puppets. If you want to know how big a real one was, see [[@trex-compare|T. rex compared]].

Later, motion capture let actors wear suits covered in dots while cameras tracked their movements. Computers used that data to move a digital creature, so a human performance drives a character who is not human at all. Today, Indian films such as *Baahubali* (2015) used hundreds of VFX artists, and Indian studios also work on many big Hollywood films.

Some effects are sounds. Footsteps, rustling clothes and creaking doors are often recorded later by Foley artists, named after the American sound expert Jack Foley. Squeezing cornflour in a bag can sound like walking on snow, and snapping celery can sound like breaking bones.

In films made in [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] and in Mumbai, the same scene may have dozens of these sounds layered together. When they are missing, a scene can feel strangely empty, even if the pictures look perfect.

text: अब तक नापी गई किसी इंसान की सबसे तेज़ दौड़ लगभग 44 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की है। उसेन बोल्ट ने यह रफ़्तार 2009 की बर्लिन विश्व चैंपियनशिप में 100 मीटर के अपने विश्व रिकॉर्ड, 9.58 सेकंड, के बीच में छुई थी। 2026 में भी यह रिकॉर्ड कायम था। ज़्यादातर फ़िट बड़े लोगों की सबसे तेज़ रफ़्तार 20 से 30 किमी प्रति घंटे के बीच कहीं रहती है।

क्या इंसान और तेज़ दौड़ सकते हैं? शायद थोड़ा-सा। प्रयोगशाला के अध्ययन बताते हैं कि असली हद हमारी टाँगों की ताकत नहीं, बल्कि यह है कि हमारी [[@muscles|मांसपेशियाँ]] कितनी जल्दी चालू और बंद हो सकती हैं। कुछ वैज्ञानिक सोचते हैं कि एक आदर्श धावक किसी दिन 50 किमी प्रति घंटे या उससे ज़्यादा तक पहुँच सकता है, जबकि दूसरे सोचते हैं कि हम पहले ही छत के करीब हैं।

2010 में अमेरिका के टेक्सस की सदर्न मेथडिस्ट यूनिवर्सिटी के शोधकर्ताओं ने धावकों को एक खास ट्रेडमिल पर दौड़ाया, जो नापता था कि वे उस पर कितनी ज़ोर से पैर पटकते हैं। सबसे तेज़ रफ़्तार पर भी धावक अपनी टाँगों की पूरी ताकत के आसपास नहीं थे। असली ब्रेक समय था। मांसपेशियों के रेशों को सिकुड़ने के लिए एक पल चाहिए, और 44 किमी प्रति घंटे पर इतना समय होता ही नहीं। शोधकर्ताओं का अनुमान था कि अगर मांसपेशियाँ और तेज़ी से काम कर सकें, तो सिद्धांत रूप में हमारी टाँगें हमें लगभग 60 किमी प्रति घंटे तक ले जा सकती हैं।

इतनी जल्दी किसी को इसकी उम्मीद नहीं। अब रिकॉर्ड सेकंड के सौवें हिस्सों से टूटते हैं। बेहतर जूते, ज़्यादा लचीले ट्रैक और प्रशिक्षण का विज्ञान मदद करते हैं, जो [[@sport-science-sprinting|फ़र्राटा दौड़ के विज्ञान]] की कहानी है।

sec.h: इंसान दूर तक जाने के लिए बने हैं

100 मीटर में एक [[@cheetah-return|चीता]] 90 किमी प्रति घंटे से ज़्यादा की रफ़्तार से किसी भी ओलंपिक चैंपियन की नाक कटवा देगा। पर किसी गर्म दोपहर में 30 किलोमीटर की दौड़ में कहानी पलट जाती है। चीते लगभग एक मिनट के पीछा करने में ही गरम होकर हाँफने लगते हैं। इंसान पूरे शरीर पर [[@sweat|पसीने]] से गर्मी निकाल सकते हैं, और दौड़ते हुए खुलकर साँस ले सकते हैं। यहीं इंसान की [[endurance|सहनशक्ति]] काम आती है।

कुछ वैज्ञानिक सोचते हैं कि शुरुआती इंसानों ने शिकार के लिए इसका इस्तेमाल किया। वे भरी दोपहर की गर्मी में किसी हिरण का पीछा करते रहते, जब तक वह थककर गिर न जाए। कालाहारी रेगिस्तान के शिकारियों जैसे कुछ समूहों को आधुनिक समय में भी ऐसा करते दर्ज किया गया है।

इतनी बढ़त में [[energy|ऊर्जा]] खर्च होती है। अमेरिका की नॉर्थवेस्टर्न यूनिवर्सिटी के वैज्ञानिकों ने 2014 में हिसाब लगाया कि लगभग 4 और 5 साल की उम्र में दिमाग उस ऊर्जा का लगभग दो-तिहाई इस्तेमाल करता है जो शरीर आराम करते समय जलाता है। उन्होंने देखा कि यही वह समय है जब बच्चों की लंबाई बढ़ने की रफ़्तार धीमी हो जाती है, और अनुमान लगाया कि शायद शरीर दिमाग के लिए ऊर्जा बचा रहा है।

अमेरिका में हुए शोध, खासकर वॉशिंगटन यूनिवर्सिटी की पैट्रिशिया कूल के काम, से पता चला कि बहुत छोटे बच्चे किसी भी भाषा की ध्वनियों में फ़र्क पहचान सकते हैं। लगभग पहले जन्मदिन तक वे आसपास बोली जाने वाली भाषाओं की ध्वनियों में माहिर होते जाते हैं, और बाकी में कमज़ोर।

बच्चे सालों तक आसानी से [[@learning-languages|भाषाएँ सीख]] सकते हैं। भारत जैसे देश के लिए यह अच्छी बात है, जहाँ बहुत-से बच्चे दो-तीन भाषाएँ बोलते हुए बड़े होते हैं। [[@bilingual-brain|कई भाषाओं]] के बीच बड़े होने से दिमाग उलझता नहीं। बच्चे उन्हें अपने-आप अलग-अलग पहचान लेते हैं।

[[@puberty-basics|किशोरावस्था]] में दिमाग बदलाव के एक और बड़े दौर से गुज़रता है। भावनाओं और इनाम से जुड़े हिस्से बहुत सक्रिय हो जाते हैं, जबकि माथे के पीछे का प्रीफ़्रंटल कॉर्टेक्स अभी भी तारों से जुड़ रहा होता है। यह अगला हिस्सा योजना बनाने, धैर्य रखने और खतरे को तौलने में मदद करता है।

वैज्ञानिक सोचते हैं कि यह बेमेल शायद समझाता है कि किशोरों को रोमांच, नए अनुभव और दोस्तों के साथ समय बिताना इतना क्यों भाता है। इसी वजह से किशोर उम्र नए हुनर सीखने का बढ़िया समय भी है, संगीत से कोडिंग और खेल तक।

कोई जादुई तरकीब नहीं है, पर बुनियादी बातें बहुत मायने रखती हैं। [[@sleep-why|नींद]] वह समय है जब दिमाग दिन भर में सीखी बातों को छाँटकर सहेजता है, इसीलिए बच्चों को बड़ों से ज़्यादा नींद चाहिए। खाना भी मायने रखता है, क्योंकि दिमाग उन्हीं [[nutrient|पोषक तत्वों]] से बनता है जो तुम खाते हो। खेलना, पढ़ना, परिवार से बातें करना, बाहर घूमना-फिरना और नई चीज़ें आज़माना, ये सब दिमाग को करने के लिए नया काम देते हैं।

दिमाग ज़िंदगी भर बदलता भी रहता है। वैज्ञानिक इसे प्लास्टिसिटी, यानी लचीलापन, कहते हैं। नई भाषा या नया वाद्य सीखता बड़ा भी नए जोड़ बनाता है। बस आम तौर पर उसे बच्चे से ज़्यादा मेहनत करनी पड़ती है।

text: Not the way films show it. No machine can read your secret thoughts or dreams. But computers can now pick up certain brain signals and turn them into actions. People who cannot move have used brain implants to type, move a robotic arm, play video games and even speak through a computer voice.

These systems are called brain-computer interfaces. They work by listening to the tiny electrical pulses that brain cells use to talk to each other. A computer learns which patterns mean "move left" or "say hello", then carries them out.

sec.t:
Your brain has around 86 billion [[neuron|neurons]], cells that send messages using small electrical pulses. When you decide to move your hand, a pattern of pulses fires in an area near the top of your head. Those signals travel down your [[@nervous-system|nerves]] to your muscles.

In 1924, German doctor Hans Berger placed electrodes on a person's head and recorded faint brain waves for the first time. This method, called EEG, is still used in hospitals today. It is a bit like listening to a cricket stadium from outside. You can hear the crowd roar, but not individual conversations.

sec.h: Can it guess what you are thinking?
sec.t:
In 2023, scientists at the University of Texas used a large brain scanner called fMRI and an AI system to guess what stories people were listening to. It got the gist, but not the exact words. It needed each person to lie in the scanner for about 16 hours to train it. It failed when people deliberately thought about something else.

That is the key point. Today's devices need training with a willing person, and they only decode certain kinds of signals. Thinking is spread across the whole brain in ways scientists still do not fully understand.

Even so, some people worry. Simple EEG headbands are already sold for gaming, meditation and focus. Companies could collect brain data the way apps collect your location. In 2021, Chile became the first country to protect "neural rights" in its [[constitution|constitution]]. In 2024, the US state of Colorado passed a law treating brain data as private, like fingerprints.

Indian scientists are working on brain-computer research too, at places like IIT Kanpur and the National Brain Research Centre near Delhi. Most of this work aims to help people with strokes or spinal injuries.

The big question is how to share the benefits while keeping minds private, a debate about [[@privacy|privacy]] that is only beginning. Some engineers are already joining brain signals to [[@prosthetics|robotic limbs]] that can send a sense of touch back to the user. And the AI systems that decode the signals are built from layers of maths loosely inspired by brain cells, called [[@neural-networks|neural networks]].

text: Future medicine is already arriving. Doctors can now edit faulty [[gene|genes]] inside a patient's cells to treat some inherited diseases. [[vaccine|Vaccines]] can be designed in days using a molecule called mRNA. A patient's own immune cells can be trained in a lab to fight cancer. Robots help surgeons make tiny, precise cuts, and AI helps read scans.

Other ideas are still being tested. Scientists are trying to 3D-print living tissue, grow replacement organs and build microscopic robots that deliver medicine. Some of these may take decades. A few may never work. But medicine is changing faster now than at almost any time in history.

sec.t:
Every cell carries [[@dna|DNA]], a long code of instructions. A single wrong letter can cause disease. Sickle cell disease, which affects millions of people in Africa, India and among African Americans, comes from one such error. It bends red blood cells into a crescent shape, causing pain and damage.

In 2023, Britain and then the US approved Casgevy, the first medicine made with the gene-editing tool CRISPR. Doctors take stem cells from the patient's bone marrow, edit them in a lab and put them back. Early results show many patients free of painful crises. It is very expensive, though, and treatment takes months.

CAR-T therapy turns a patient's own white blood cells into cancer hunters. The cells are collected, given new instructions in a lab, multiplied and put back. For some blood cancers, it can work when nothing else has.

In the US, this therapy can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. In 2023, India approved NexCAR19, developed by IIT Bombay and Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai. It costs far less, which could make the treatment possible for many more families.

sec.h: Robots and AI in the room
sec.t:
[[surgeon|Surgeons]] in many big hospitals, including in India, use robotic systems. The surgeon sits at a console and controls thin robot arms that hold tiny tools and a camera. The robot doesn't decide anything. It steadies the surgeon's hand and lets them work through very small cuts, so patients often heal faster.

AI systems are learning to spot signs of disease in X-rays, eye scans and skin photos. In trials, some match expert doctors at certain tasks. They're best used as a second pair of eyes, with a doctor making the final decision. In places with few specialists, like many rural districts in India, such tools could help spot problems early.

Researchers are printing layers of living cells to make patches of skin and [[cartilage|cartilage]]. Whole working organs, like a printed kidney, are still far off. Scientists are also growing organs in pigs whose genes are edited so the human body won't reject them. In 2024, surgeons in the US transplanted gene-edited pig kidneys into living patients.

And "nanobots", robots smaller than a cell, swimming through blood to deliver medicine? Labs have made tiny moving particles, but they are still experiments. Medicine has always had bold dreamers, though. More than 2,000 years ago, the Indian surgeon [[@sushruta|Sushruta]] described ways to rebuild a damaged nose using skin from the cheek, an idea modern plastic surgeons still recognise.

text: The Bronze Age was the long stretch of time when the most important material for tools and weapons was bronze. Bronze is an [[alloy|alloy]], a mixture of metals: mostly copper with a little tin. It is much harder than pure copper and holds a sharp edge.

In West Asia, the Bronze Age began around 3300 BCE and lasted about 2,000 years. It came after the [[@stone-age|Stone Age]] and before the [[@iron-age|Iron Age]]. During it, people built great cities, invented writing and set up trade routes across seas and deserts.

myth: The Bronze Age started at the same moment all over the world.

Bronze-making began in West Asia around 3300 BCE, reached Britain around 2500 BCE, and never really happened in some places, which went from stone tools almost straight to iron. The "ages" are labels historians use, not dates on a world calendar.

sec.t:
People had worked copper for thousands of years before bronze. But copper is soft. A copper axe bends and blunts quickly. Somewhere in West Asia, metalworkers learned that melting in some tin made a far tougher metal.

Bronze could be poured into moulds of clay or stone, so the same shape could be made again and again. Farmers got better sickles and ploughs. Carpenters got chisels and saws. Armies got swords, spearheads and helmets. Bronze also made beautiful things: mirrors, bells, jewellery and statues.

In China, bronze-workers of the Shang [[dynasty|dynasty]], more than 3,000 years ago, cast huge [[ritual|ritual]] vessels for food and wine, some heavier than a small car. In Europe, people buried bronze swords and shields in rivers and bogs, perhaps as gifts to their gods. Because bronze was valuable, old tools were often melted down and recast, so the objects that survive are only a small share of what was made.

{{story:bronze-casting}}

The cities of Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, in today's Pakistan and India, were a Bronze Age [[civilisation|civilisation]]. Their people made copper and bronze tools, fish-hooks, razors and pots. The most famous object is a small bronze figure called the Dancing Girl, about 4,500 years old and only 10.5 cm tall. She stands with one hand on her hip, wearing a stack of bangles on her arm.

She was made by the lost-wax method. A model is shaped in wax, covered in clay and heated, so the wax melts away and leaves a hollow mould. Craftspeople making [[@dhokra|dhokra]] figures in Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal still use a version of this method today.

Copper is found in many places, but tin is not. Mesopotamia had no tin of its own. Traders brought it from far away, possibly from Central Asia. Indus cities traded with Mesopotamia too, sending beads, cotton and other goods by sea along the [[@harappan-trade|Harappan trade]] routes.

In 1982, a sponge diver spotted strange metal "biscuits" on the seabed off Uluburun in southern Turkey. They turned out to be the cargo of a ship that sank around 1300 BCE. On board were about ten tonnes of copper ingots and one tonne of tin, almost exactly the right mix for bronze. There were also ebony, ivory, glass and a gold scarab from Egypt. It is one of the richest ancient wrecks ever found.

Around 1200 BCE, many kingdoms around the eastern Mediterranean fell apart within a few decades. Cities were burned, trade routes broke and writing vanished from some regions. Historians still argue about why. [[drought|Drought]], earthquakes, raiders called the "Sea Peoples" and rebellions are all suspects, and it was probably several at once.

When trade broke down, tin became even harder to get. Iron ore, on the other hand, is found almost everywhere. Smiths who learned to work it no longer had to wait for ships from far away. Slowly, iron took over, and the Bronze Age gave way to a new one.

The idea of a Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age came from Christian Jürgensen Thomsen, a Danish museum curator. In the early 1800s he sorted his museum's objects by what they were made of, and in 1836 he published the idea. The labels stuck and are still used, even though the real story is messier than three neat boxes.

text: The French Revolution was a period of upheaval in France from 1789 to 1799. Ordinary people, lawyers and some nobles rose against an unfair system in which the king held most power and nobles and clergy paid few taxes.

In ten years, the revolutionaries ended the [[monarchy|monarchy]], executed the king, wrote a famous declaration of rights and tried out new ideas about government. The revolution also brought violence, war and a period of fear called the Terror. In 1799 the general Napoleon Bonaparte seized power. Its slogan, "Liberty, equality, fraternity", is still France's motto.

myth: Queen Marie Antoinette said "Let them eat cake" when told the poor had no bread.
There is no evidence she ever said it. A similar line appears in the writings of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, about an unnamed "great princess", written when Marie Antoinette was still a child in Austria.

sec.t:
In the 1780s, French society was divided into three "estates". The clergy were the First Estate, and nobles the Second. Everyone else, about 97 per cent of people, from rich merchants to poor peasants, made up the Third Estate. The Third Estate paid most of the taxes.

The government was nearly bankrupt, partly because France had spent heavily helping the Americans win the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]]. In 1788 bad harvests made bread, the main food of the poor, very expensive. Meanwhile, writers of the Enlightenment had spread ideas that power should come from the people, not from kings chosen by God.

In August 1789, the new National Assembly issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. It said that people are born and remain free and equal in rights, and that power belongs to the nation.

Not everyone was included. In 1791 the writer Olympe de Gouges published her own Declaration of the Rights of Woman, arguing that women deserved the same rights. Enslaved people in French colonies were also left out at first, until the enslaved people of Saint-Domingue rose up in the [[@haitian-revolution|Haitian Revolution]]. In 1794 France abolished slavery in its colonies, though Napoleon later brought it back.

Europe's kings feared the revolution would spread. War broke out in 1792. Accused of plotting with France's enemies, Louis XVI lost his throne, and in January 1793 he was executed by guillotine.

A group led by Maximilien Robespierre then took control. In 1793–94, during the Terror, they arrested people suspected of opposing the revolution. Around 17,000 people were officially sentenced to death, and many more died in prison or in fighting inside France. In July 1794 Robespierre himself was overthrown and executed.

Some changes from these years still shape daily life. The revolutionaries wanted measurements that were the same everywhere and based on nature. They defined the metre as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the [[equator|equator]]. Over the next two centuries, the [[@metric-system|metric system]] spread around the world, including to India.

After the Terror, a weak government struggled on, until Napoleon took power in 1799. The ideas of the revolution, that citizens have rights and that power should come from the people, inspired movements far beyond France, including later freedom struggles in Latin America and Asia.

text: Angkor Wat is a vast stone temple in northern Cambodia, near the town of Siem Reap. It was built in the early 1100s by King Suryavarman II of the [[@khmer-empire|Khmer Empire]], as a temple to the Hindu god Vishnu. Over time, it became a Buddhist temple, and it still is one today.

It is the largest religious monument in the world. Its outer walls and moat enclose an area of about 160 hectares, roughly the size of 200 football fields. In the middle rise five towers shaped like lotus buds. They are meant to stand for Mount Meru, the home of the gods in Hindu and Buddhist belief. Angkor Wat is so important to Cambodians that it appears on the national flag.

sec.h: A temple shaped like the universe
sec.t:
The whole design is a model of the universe as described in Hindu texts. The central tower is Mount Meru. The four smaller towers are surrounding peaks. The walls stand for the mountains at the edge of the world, and the wide moat for the ocean beyond.

Unusually, Angkor Wat faces west, while most Khmer temples face east. Scholars have suggested reasons. West is the direction linked with Vishnu, and some think the temple was also meant as the king's tomb.

The temple is built of sandstone blocks brought from a quarry in the Kulen hills, about 40 km away. Experts think the blocks were moved partly by canals and rafts, then pulled on land.

Angkor Wat was only one part of a huge city. The Khmer built giant [[reservoir|reservoirs]], called barays, and canals to store and spread water for rice fields. In 2012, and again in 2015, scientists flew over the area with [[@lasers|lasers]], a method called lidar, which can see through trees to the ground. They found roads, ponds and neighbourhoods hidden under the forest, showing that greater Angkor was one of the largest cities of its time. [[@archaeology|Archaeology]] has rarely had a better tool.

Merchants, priests and travellers carried Hindu and Buddhist ideas from India across South-East Asia over many centuries. Khmer kings used [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] names and titles, and built temples to Vishnu and Shiva in their own style.

India's link to the temple continued in modern times. From 1986 to 1993, the Archaeological Survey of India worked on cleaning and repairing parts of Angkor Wat, though some of its cleaning methods were later criticised. Many countries now help to look after Angkor together.

The Khmer capital moved south in the 1400s, and many of Angkor's temples were swallowed by forest, as told in [[@lost-cities|lost cities]]. At the nearby temple of Ta Prohm, giant tree roots still grip the stones.

Angkor Wat itself was never abandoned. Today it is a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], and crowds gather before dawn to watch the Sun rise behind its towers, reflected in the pools in front.

text: Puducherry feels French because France ruled it, on and off, for nearly 300 years. French traders arrived in 1674, and the town became the capital of French India. When India won independence from Britain in 1947, Puducherry stayed French. It only joined India in 1954.

The French left their mark in the town's layout, buildings, food and even its police uniforms. In the old French Quarter, streets run in a neat grid, lined with yellow and white [[colonial|colonial]] houses with tall shuttered windows and bougainvillea spilling over the walls. Signs carry French street names. Bakeries sell croissants beside idli and vada.

sec.h: A French town in Tamil country
sec.t:
In 1674, François Martin set up a French trading post on the Coromandel Coast, in what is now Tamil Nadu, about 150 km south of today's [[@chennai|Chennai]]. The British were already based in Chennai, then called Madras, so the two rivals were close neighbours. The French East India Company traded cloth, spices and indigo, and Pondichéry grew into a fortified town. The British and the French fought over it several times, and the British captured and largely destroyed it in 1761. It was handed back and rebuilt.

French India eventually had five main settlements: Pondichéry, Karaikal, Mahe, Yanam and Chandernagore in Bengal. They were tiny compared with British India. Chandernagore joined India in 1950 and later became part of West Bengal.

After 1947, India asked France to hand over its settlements. France held talks with local leaders, and on 1 November 1954, Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam were transferred to India in practice. The formal [[treaty|treaty]] was ratified in 1962. Unlike [[@goa-liberation|Goa]], which Portugal refused to give up until 1961, the French handover happened peacefully.

The four parts stayed together as one union [[territory|territory]], even though they are far apart. Mahe is on the Kerala coast, Yanam is in Andhra Pradesh, and Karaikal and Puducherry are in Tamil Nadu. People there could choose French or Indian citizenship, and some families kept French passports. The town was renamed Puducherry, its Tamil name meaning "new town", in 2006.

In 1910, Sri Aurobindo, a revolutionary who had become a spiritual teacher, came to Pondicherry to escape arrest by the British in Bengal. He stayed and founded an ashram, joined by a French woman, Mirra Alfassa, known as "the Mother".

In 1968, she founded Auroville nearby, an experimental township meant for people from all countries to live together. At its centre stands the Matrimandir, a huge golden globe used for silent [[@mindfulness|meditation]]. Around it, residents from dozens of countries have planted forests on what was once dry, bare land, turning the red earth green.

text: Stonehenge is a [[prehistoric|prehistoric]] monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. It is a ring of giant standing stones, some with huge flat stones balanced across their tops like lintels over a doorway. It was built in stages, starting about 5,000 years ago, by farming people of the [[@stone-age|Stone Age]].

Nobody left a written explanation, because the builders had no writing. But [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] have worked out a great deal from the stones, bones, tools and holes in the ground. Stonehenge was lined up with the Sun at midsummer and midwinter, and it was used as a burial place. It was almost certainly a place for ceremonies, where people gathered at special times of the year.

d.try: On a sunny day, push a stick upright into the ground or into a pot of soil. Mark the tip of its shadow with a pebble every hour. Watch how the shadow moves and shrinks around midday. Stonehenge's builders lined up their stones with the Sun's movements in a similar way.
myth: Stonehenge was built by the Druids.
Druids were priests in Iron Age Britain, about 2,000 years ago. Stonehenge was built more than 2,000 years before that. The link was made by writers in the 1600s and 1700s, and it stuck.

sec.t:
At first, around 3000 BCE, Stonehenge was a circular ditch and bank, with a ring of pits. Some held the cremated remains of people, which makes it one of Britain's earliest large cemeteries.

About 2500 BCE, the builders raised the big stones. The large blocks are a hard local rock called sarsen. The tallest stand about 7 m above the ground, and the heaviest weighs more than 30 tonnes, as much as five adult elephants. Smaller "bluestones" were set up among them and rearranged several times over the following centuries.

In 2020, scientists compared the chemistry of the sarsens with rocks across southern England. Most matched an area called West Woods, about 25 km north. The bluestones came from much further away, the Preseli Hills of Wales, about 225 km off.

In 2024, researchers found that the flat Altar Stone at the centre came from north-east [[@scotland|Scotland]], about 750 km away. Nobody yet knows whether it travelled overland or by boat along the coast. Either way, it shows that people across Britain were connected 5,000 years ago.

Stonehenge is arranged so that on midsummer morning, the Sun rises close to a stone outside the circle, called the Heel Stone. On midwinter evening, it sets in line with the monument from the other side.

Many experts think the midwinter sunset was the most important moment. Pig bones found at a nearby settlement suggest big feasts were held there in winter.

The builders were Neolithic farmers, people who kept cattle and pigs and grew crops. Some archaeologists think the workers lived at a big village called Durrington Walls, about 3 km away.

Today thousands of people still gather at Stonehenge for sunrise at the summer [[solstice|solstice]]. The monument is cared for by English Heritage, and since 1986 it has been a [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]].
